summary: Sets out the compliance statements for the CMC certificate enrollment protocol, saying what an implementation must support to be considered compliant. The data structures and transports are covered in other documents; this one pulls together what is needed for interoperability. It was replaced by RFC 10004.

plainLanguage.summary: CMC is the protocol a program uses to ask for a certificate. This RFC lists what a program that wants to be a good CMC citizen has to do: which message formats to accept, which controls to send, and which encryption and signature algorithms to handle.

questions: what must a cmc implementation support
subtitle: The checklist of what a certificate-enrollment client, registration authority or CA must support to count as compliant CMC.

tldr.problem: The CMC certificate enrollment protocol has its structures and transport in separate documents. Without one agreed checklist, two implementations could each claim to be correct and still fail to talk to each other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states, per role, exactly which request formats, transport mechanisms, controls and cryptographic algorithms an implementation must, should or may support, using the RFC 2119 requirement words.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5274 was a Proposed Standard. It has been obsoleted by RFC 10004 and updated by RFC 6402.

sections.title: The CMC Chain of Client and Server
sections.content:
The CMC protocol, Certificate Management over CMS, is designed in terms of a client and server relationship. In the simplest case the client is the requestor of the certificate, that is the End Entity, and the server is the issuer of the certificate, that is the Certification Authority.

The introduction of a Registration Authority into the set of agents complicates the picture only slightly. The RA becomes the server with respect to the certificate requestor, and it becomes the client with respect to the certificate issuer. Any number of RAs can be inserted into the picture in this manner.

The RAs may serve specialized purposes that are not currently covered by this document. One such purpose would be a key escrow agent. All certificate requests for encryption keys would be directed through such an RA, and it would take appropriate action to do the key archival. Key recovery requests could be defined in the CMC methodology, allowing the key escrow agent to perform that operation while acting as the final server in the chain of agents.

If there are multiple RAs in the system, it is considered normal that not all RAs will see all certificate requests. The routing between the RAs may be dependent on the content of the certificate requests involved.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the program holding the key asks the authority that signs certificates. A registration authority can sit in between, so the requester talks to the RA and the RA talks to the CA.

sections.title: The Roles and the Vocabulary
sections.content:
The RFC defines the terms it uses. The End-Entity is the entity that owns a key pair and for whom a certificate is issued. The Registration Authority, or local RA, is an entity that acts as an intermediary between the End-Entity and the CA. Multiple RAs can exist between the End-Entity and the Certification Authority, and RAs may perform additional services such as key generation or key archival. The Certification Authority is the entity that issues certificates.

A Client is an entity that creates a PKI Request, and in this document both RAs and EEs can be clients. A Server is an entity that processes PKI Requests and creates PKI Responses, and both CAs and RAs can be servers. A PKI Request includes certification requests and revocation requests; a PKI Response includes certs-only messages and failure messages.

Two security terms matter for the requirements that follow. Proof-of-Identity refers to the client proving they are who they say they are to the server. Proof-of-Possession refers to a value that can be used to prove that the private key corresponding to a public key is in the possession of, and can be used by, the end-entity. The RFC also names PKCS #10, the certification request syntax, CRMF, the Certificate Request Message Format, CMS, the Cryptographic Message Syntax, and the transport wrapper, the outermost CMS wrapping layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different proofs are used. One shows who the requester is; the other shows the requester really holds the private key the certificate will be issued for.

sections.title: Requirements for All Entities
sections.content:
Unless specifically stated otherwise, all of the compliance statements in the CMC structures and transport documents must be adhered to.

All entities must support Full PKI Requests, Simple PKI Responses and Full PKI Responses, while servers should support Simple PKI Requests. All entities must support the CRMF syntax for certification requests, and support for the PKCS #10 syntax for certification requests should be implemented by servers. The extendedFailInfo field should not be populated in the CMCStatusInfoV2 object; the failInfo field should be used to relay this information, and if extendedFailInfo is used it is suggested that an additional CMCStatusInfoV2 item exist for the same body part with a failInfo field.

All entities must implement the HTTP transport mechanism, while other transport mechanisms may be implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: The baseline is the same for everyone: handle the full request and response formats, use the CRMF request syntax, and speak over HTTP.

sections.title: Cryptographic Algorithm Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC then fixes the algorithms. All entities must verify DSA-SHA1 and RSA-SHA1 signatures in SignedData, and may verify other signature algorithms. It is strongly suggested that RSA-PSS with SHA-1 be verified, and strongly suggested that SHA-256 using RSA and RSA-PSS be verified. All entities must generate either DSA-SHA1 or RSA-SHA1 signatures for SignedData, while other signature algorithms may be used for generation.

All entities must support the Advanced Encryption Standard as the content encryption algorithm for EnvelopedData, and must support RSA as a key transport algorithm for EnvelopedData; they should support RSA-OAEP. If an entity supports key agreement for EnvelopedData, it must support Diffie-Hellman. If it supports PasswordRecipientInfo for EnvelopedData or AuthenticatedData, it must support PBKDF2 for key derivation algorithms and must support AES key wrap as the key encryption algorithm. If AuthenticatedData is supported, PasswordRecipientInfo must be supported.

Per-control requirements follow the same pattern. For the Identity Proof Version 2 control, SHA-1 must be implemented for the hash algorithm and SHA-256 should be implemented; HMAC-SHA1 must be implemented for the message authentication code algorithm and HMAC-SHA256 should be implemented. The Pop Link Witness Version 2 control has the same shape, plus PBKDF2 as an optional key generation algorithm. The Encrypted POP and Decrypted POP controls require SHA-1 for the witness algorithm and HMAC-SHA1 for the POP algorithm, with SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA256 recommended. The Publish Trust Anchors control requires SHA-1 for its hash algorithm, with SHA-256 recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithms are pinned so that one vendor's client can always read another's message. Older algorithms are mandatory for reading, newer ones are recommended for writing.

sections.title: The Table of Required Controls
sections.content:
The controls are the tagged pieces of information carried inside a CMC message, and the RFC gives a table of the required level of support for each one, per role. Extended CMC Status Info and the Identity Proof Version 2, Identification, POP Link Random and POP Link Witness Version 2 controls are MUST for the End-Entity, the RA and the CA alike, as are Data Return, Transaction ID, Sender Nonce, Recipient Nonce, Query Pending and Confirm Certificate Acceptance.

The requirements differ where the roles differ. The Modify Cert Request control does not apply to an End-Entity and is MUST for an RA; the RA POP Witness control does not apply to an End-Entity and is SHOULD for an RA; Revocation Request is SHOULD for an End-Entity and an RA but MUST for a CA. Get Certificate, Get CRL and Publication Information are optional for all three roles. The notes to the table qualify several entries: CAs should implement a control if designed to work with RAs, and must implement it if designed to work with RAs; implementation of Publish Trust Anchors and Authenticate Data is optional, but strongly suggested, because they give a simple way to distribute trust anchors into clients without user intervention; and the Encrypted and Decrypted POP controls are needed by an End-Entity only if it supports key agreement algorithms or needs to operate where the hardware keys cannot provide proof of possession.

Further requirements narrow the CRMF features that may be used. The id-regCtrl-regToken and id-regCtrl-authToken tokens must not be used, since the CMC controls identification and identityProof perform the same service and are more specifically defined. The id-regCtrl-pkiArchiveOptions token should not be supported, because an alternative method is under development. The behaviour of id-regCtrl-oldCertID is not presently used; it is replaced by issuing the new certificate and using the id-cmc-publishCert control to remove the old certificate from publication. The id-regCtrl-protocolEncrKey token is not used.
sections.plainLanguage: Each control is a labelled chunk of information in the message. The table says which ones each role has to send or understand, and it differs for the three roles in a few places.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC uses the CMC structures and transport documents as building blocks, and includes their security sections by reference. It then adds its own point: knowledge of how an entity is expected to operate is vital in determining which sections of requirements are applicable to that entity, and care needs to be taken in determining which sections apply and fully implementing the necessary code.

The final paragraph is a warning about the algorithm list itself. Cryptographic algorithms have and will be broken or weakened. Implementers and users need to check that the cryptographic algorithms listed in this document make sense from a security level. The IETF may from time to time issue documents dealing with the current state of the art, and the RFC names two examples, on small subgroups and on hash attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Getting the rules right for your own role is part of the security, and the algorithm list itself ages: check it against the current guidance.

items.title: End-Entity (EE)
items.text: Owns the key pair and is the one the certificate is issued for.

items.title: Registration Authority (RA)
items.text: Sits between the End-Entity and the CA, acting as server to the former and client to the latter.

items.title: Certification Authority (CA)
items.text: Issues the certificates and enforces proof of possession before it does.
